title: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines

paper.title: The Coordination Tax and the Heterogeneity Dividend: Break-Even Conditions for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
paper.abstract: Abstract Multi-agent LLM pipelines built on interoperability protocols such as the Open Floor Protocol (OFP) or A2A are usually justified on capability grounds, with their runtime cost treated as an overhead of unknown size. Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax – decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost – against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound, α < 1 / r \alpha<1/r , and measure every term, with OFP as the protocol under test, on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs of six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. Decomposition does not pay on these tasks: a planner–coder–reviewer pipeline costs 3.22 × \times as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24 × \times as long, and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the pipeline’s cost to 0.39 × \times but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, leaving it dearer, slower and less accurate than the single call, and the break-even forecast misses by -19% because the cheap roles inflate token volume. The saving lies in choosing a model per task instead: an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call’s cost per solved task. Keywords: Multi-agent LLM systems, Voice agents, Agent interoperability, Open Floor Protocol, LLM routing, Cost-aware evaluation, Benchmarking, Agent Harness

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Interoperability protocols for autonomous agents are arriving faster than the evidence for them. The Open Floor Protocol (OFP) [ 22 ] standardises a conversational floor over which heterogeneous agents exchange JSON envelopes; A2A [ 18 ] standardises peer-to-peer agent task delegation; the Model Context Protocol [ 1 ] standardises the agent-to-tool boundary. Each is argued for on the same grounds: agents built on different stacks can discover one another, compose across organisational boundaries, and be replaced independently. Each is deployed on the tacit assumption that the runtime price of that flexibility is small enough not to matter. The assumption is rarely tested. Practitioners ask a blunter question instead – is a multi-agent pipeline simply slower and more expensive than one call to the model? – and the answer usually offered is a benchmark number for one task, one model and one architecture. The question matters most for voice agents. OFP grew out of the effort to let conversational and voice assistants from different vendors work together [ 21 , 7 , 9 ] , and a voice agent is judged turn by turn: whatever time the agents spend coordinating behind the scenes delays the spoken reply the user is waiting for. For such agents latency counts as much as spend, and any overhead that a protocol or a decomposition adds is paid inside the conversational turn. That comparison conflates three mechanisms that move cost in different directions and at different magnitudes. Decomposition splits one generation into several, re-establishing context at every stage and inflating total token volume. The protocol layer adds serialisation, envelope construction, transport and floor management at every handoff. Model heterogeneity allows each role to be served by a different model, so that mechanical roles can be pushed onto cheaper and faster models while only the roles that need frontier capability pay frontier prices. Only the third mechanism can be negative, and it is available exclusively to the decomposed architecture. A benchmark that holds the model fixed across pipeline stages therefore measures the cost of decomposition and the protocol tax while deliberately discarding the only source of saving – and then reports the sum as the cost of the protocol. This paper reframes the question as an economic one. We ask under what conditions the heterogeneity dividend exceeds the coordination tax, derive those conditions in closed form, and measure every parameter in them. The target is a statement of the form: for a decomposition overhead of α \alpha , a cheap/strong price ratio of r r , and a routable work fraction f f , protocol-mediated decomposition is cheaper than a single strong call if and only if f f exceeds an explicit threshold – and is never cheaper, at any f f , once α \alpha exceeds 1 / r 1/r . That statement is protocol-agnostic and survives the next protocol, which a raw benchmark number does not. It is also falsifiable, and we test it. Our contributions are: • a closed-form model of the coordination tax and the heterogeneity dividend, with a cost break-even threshold, a feasibility bound, a latency condition and a misrouting term, and a reporting rule that splits any heterogeneous-versus-uniform cost ratio into a volume factor and a price factor (Section 3 ); • a six-condition design that separates decomposition, protocol and model assignment, and includes the two baselines an economic claim has to beat: one call on the cheap model, and a router (Section 4 ); • a direct measurement of an interoperability protocol’s per-handoff runtime overhead, timed inside the convener rather than inferred from end-to-end differences (Section 5 ); • results on 135 tasks in two difficulty tiers, analysed with the task as the unit and against hypotheses fixed before data collection (Sections 4 – 6 ). Section 2 positions the work, Section 3 develops the model, Section 4 specifies the study, and Sections 5 and 6 report and discuss the results. Sections 7 – 9 cover validity, future work and reproducibility.

sections.heading: 2.1 Agent Interoperability Protocols
sections.text: The Open Floor Protocol, developed within the Open Voice Interoperability Initiative of the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation, standardises the Conversation Envelope that every agent sends and receives, Dialog Events representing what was said, Assistant Manifests describing what an agent can do, and a set of floor management events – requestFloor , grantFloor , revokeFloor , yieldFloor – by which agents built by different teams on different stacks take turns in a shared conversation [ 22 , 21 , 2 ] . Its organising metaphor is multi-party conversation: agents gather around a shared floor, and floor management – who holds it, who is invited, who is delegated to – is part of the protocol rather than of the application. This is a deliberate departure from point-to-point delegation models, and it is the feature that makes mid-task reassignment expressible at the protocol level rather than at the orchestrator level; the conception of conversational agency underlying that choice is developed in [ 15 ] . The Assistant Manifest gives discovery a declarative form, so that adding a capability is in principle a manifest change rather than a redeployment. Extensions to the floor model for managing multiparty conversations among heterogeneous assistants are developed in [ 7 , 9 ] , which sets out the delegation and convening semantics the present pipelines rely on, building on the universal open APIs for agentic multimodal communication proposed in [ 10 ] . The intellectual ancestry runs through agent communication languages such as FIPA ACL [ 6 ] , which likewise separated message structure and interaction protocol from agent internals. The modern reprise differs in that the agents are stochastic, the cost of a message is dominated by inference rather than transport, and the price of a message varies by two orders of magnitude depending on which model is behind it. That last property is what makes the economics non-trivial, and it has no analogue in the classical literature.

sections.heading: 2.2 Cost-Aware Serving: Cascades and Routers
sections.text: A parallel line of work treats model choice itself as the optimisation variable. FrugalGPT [ 3 ] cascades queries through progressively more expensive models with a learned stopping rule, reporting large cost reductions at matched quality. RouteLLM [ 20 ] trains a router that dispatches each query to a strong or a weak model based on predicted difficulty. Both establish that heterogeneous serving is where the money is; neither involves decomposition, an inter-agent protocol, or more than one model per query. Semantic caching is a third lever on the same cost function, reducing generated volume rather than unit price [ 19 , 14 , 13 ] ; it is orthogonal to the comparison studied here and we hold it out of all conditions, but it shares the property, central to Section 3.7 , that savings in token volume and savings in token price must be accounted separately. This literature supplies the competitor that agent-protocol benchmarks almost always omit. If the object is to save money by using a cheaper model where a cheaper model suffices, a single-call router achieves that with no decomposition overhead and no protocol tax whatsoever. Any claim that multi-agent routing is economically motivated must therefore be made against a router baseline, not against a single strong call. We treat its omission as the central methodological gap in existing comparisons.

sections.heading: 2.3 Multi-Agent LLM Frameworks and Their Evaluation
sections.text: Frameworks such as AutoGen [ 23 ] and MetaGPT [ 16 ] popularised role-structured pipelines – planner, implementer, reviewer – and report quality gains on reasoning and code generation. Evaluation in this literature is predominantly quality-first, with cost and latency reported as secondary descriptive statistics when reported at all. Kapoor et al. [ 17 ] document the consequence: agent evaluations that do not control for cost systematically favour architectures that simply spend more inference, and accuracy-only leaderboards reward this. Their prescription – report the accuracy-cost frontier rather than a point – is the one we adopt, extended to latency and to the protocol layer specifically. Work on staged agent pipelines with explicit inter-agent measurement is closer to our setting. An OFP-mediated three-stage pipeline is instrumented in [ 12 ] so that an evaluator observes the full trace without sitting in the decision path, precisely in order to make the protocol boundary measurable rather than implicit; related work on sentinel agents in multi-agent systems [ 11 ] adopts the same separation between the agents doing the work and the agents observing it, and the Agent Status Protocol [ 8 ] proposes a lightweight specification through which agents report their state to such observers. The present study extends that instrumentation from a single pipeline to a controlled comparison of architectures and model assignments.

sections.heading: 2.4 The Gap
sections.text: What remains absent from the literature, to our knowledge, is a design that separates decomposition, protocol and model assignment as independent factors; that times the protocol’s per-handoff overhead directly instead of inferring it from noisy end-to-end differences; that includes the cheap single call and the router against which an economic claim must be made; and that evaluates on many tasks with quality off its ceiling, reporting cost per solved task rather than per attempt. That is the gap this study addresses. A comparison across protocols, and the fault-recovery, fan-out and discovery properties that motivate interoperability protocols in the first place, remain future work (Section 8 ).

sections.heading: 3.7 Separating Price from Volume
sections.text: Both conditions treat α \alpha and r r as independent, which they are not in practice. Substituting a cheap model changes token volume as well as price, and the volume change can go either way: a cheaper model may write less or reason more, and what it writes changes what the next stage is given to work with. Attributing the combined effect to price alone misstates what routing buys, because the volume component is a quality-relevant behavioural difference rather than a contractual discount – it is invisible only while pass rates sit at ceiling. Operationally, α \alpha must be measured under the model assignment being evaluated, not under a uniform one, and an observed cost ratio between heterogeneous and uniform pipelines is best reported as the product of two factors: a volume factor , the heterogeneous pipeline’s own tokens priced at the strong model’s rates relative to the uniform pipeline’s cost, and a price factor , its actual cost relative to that. Section 5 reports both, and tests how well the model forecasts when α \alpha is taken from the uniform pipeline instead.

sections.heading: 4.1 Conditions
sections.text: Six conditions run each task under a different architecture (Fig. 2 ). A issues one call to the strong model and A ′ one call to the cheap model. R is a router: the cheap model, at low reasoning effort, reads the task and answers SMALL or LARGE, and the chosen model then gets one call; any answer other than a clear SMALL goes to the strong model. B decomposes the task into three roles – planner, coder, reviewer – chained by direct API calls with no protocol layer. C runs the same three roles over OFP: each specialist is an independent BotAgent in its own process on its own port, exchanging Envelope, GrantFloorEvent, UtteranceEvent and YieldFloorEvent objects from the OFP Python package with a convener over HTTP. D is C with the cheap model as planner and reviewer and the strong model as coder. B, C and D use identical role prompts, and in all three the reviewer’s output is the code that is graded, so in D the final code passes through the cheap model. The design isolates one mechanism per contrast. B against A measures decomposition at a fixed model; C against B measures the protocol at fixed decomposition and model; D against C measures model assignment at a fixed architecture. A ′ and R are the competitors any economic claim for D has to beat: A ′ shows what the cheap model achieves alone, and R captures the heterogeneity dividend while paying neither the decomposition tax nor the protocol tax. sections.heading: 4.2 Tasks
sections.text: Tasks come from two public, MIT-licensed benchmarks, in two tiers of difficulty. The function tier draws on HumanEval [ 4 ] : one function per task, specified by its signature and docstring and graded by the task’s own check function. The class tier draws on ClassEval [ 5 ] : one class per task with several methods sharing state, specified by a skeleton with docstrings and graded by the task’s unittest classes. Decomposition has more to do in the class tier, where a plan has to cover several interacting methods. Only ClassEval tasks whose solution and tests need nothing beyond the Python standard library are eligible (88 of 100). Every reference solution was run through the grader before use – twice, or fifty times for tasks that use the random module – and tasks that did not pass every time were dropped: three ClassEval tasks, whose tests depend on the current date, the machine’s hostname and a random draw. The class tier is all 85 remaining tasks, so it involves no sampling choice; the function tier is 50 of HumanEval’s 164 tasks, drawn with a fixed seed. Both downloads are pinned by SHA-256 hash. Each spec wraps the task in one instruction line before and one after, asking for the complete code and nothing else. Generated code is graded in a separate Python process, in a fresh temporary directory, with a 30-second timeout; a run counts as solved only if every test passes.

sections.heading: 4.3 Models, Prices and Reasoning
sections.text: The strong model is Claude Opus 5.5, at $4/$20 per million input/output tokens, and the cheap model Claude Haiku 5.5, at $0.10/$0.50, 1 1 1 Standard first-party API prices, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing , accessed 15 October 2026. Haiku 5.5 is priced higher for prompts over 100,000 tokens; no prompt in this study comes close. so r in = r out = 0.025 r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0.025 . Every call is billed at its own model’s list price, and the harness records input, output and reasoning tokens, cost and model-call time for each call. Both models reason before answering by default, and Opus 5.5 does not allow reasoning to be switched off; reasoning tokens are billed as output but never appear in the response. We therefore fix reasoning effort explicitly – medium for every call except the router’s, which is low – and report reasoning tokens separately. Neither model accepts non-default sampling parameters, so repetitions sample each model’s default stochasticity. Output is capped at 16,000 tokens per call, and no prompt caching is used.

sections.heading: 4.4 Measuring the Protocol
sections.text: The convener timestamps each handoff from just before it builds the request envelope to just after it has parsed the reply. The receiving agent reports how long its model call took, and the difference is the protocol’s share of that handoff: envelope construction, JSON serialisation, the HTTP round trip, the agent’s event dispatch and floor handling, and the reply envelope. All agents run as separate processes on one host and are started once for the whole run, so process start-up never falls inside a measured handoff. Loopback HTTP without TLS or authentication is the best case for any protocol, so the measurement is a lower bound on what a cross-host or cross-organisation deployment pays.

sections.heading: 4.5 Execution and Analysis
sections.text: Each task is run 3 times under each condition, 2430 runs in all. The run proceeds in rounds: each round holds one repetition of every (task, condition) pair in a fresh random order, so that drift in provider-side latency over the hours of the run cannot line up with any condition, and a spending cap fixed in advance can only ever cut the last round short. Runs are written as they complete, and an interrupted run resumes without repeating finished work. The run paused once when the account’s API usage limit was reached and resumed without loss. In two runs a model request hung while the host was asleep and hit the client’s 10-minute timeout before a retry succeeded; their wall time measured the host rather than the model, so both were discarded and re-run, and their $0.07 is not included in the totals. The unit of analysis is the task, not the run: repetitions of one prompt measure sampling noise, not generalisation. Each task’s cost, wall time and solve rate are first averaged over its repetitions. Comparisons between conditions are paired by task. Ratios are ratios of mean per-task values, with 95% confidence intervals from 5,000 bootstrap resamples of tasks, and p p -values come from the Wilcoxon signed-rank test on per-task differences. pass@1 is the share of runs solved, and cost per solved task is total spend divided by the number of solved runs, following the cost-controlled practice of [ 17 ] . The following hypotheses, and the criterion for each, were fixed before data collection and are implemented in the released analysis script; the repository history records them in commit 85a3748 , 25 minutes before the first run. H1 (protocol). The protocol accounts for under 1% of the uniform OFP pipeline’s median wall time, and the 95% interval for C’s cost relative to B’s includes 1. H2 (model). Holding token volumes at the uniform pipeline’s per-role values and re-pricing them under D’s model assignment forecasts D’s cost relative to A to within 15% of the observed ratio. H3 (economics). The single cheap call A ′ has a lower cost per solved task than the mixed pipeline D in both tiers. H4 (quality). On class-level tasks, the OFP pipeline C solves more tasks than the single strong call A (paired by task, p < 0.05 p<0.05 ).

sections.heading: 5.1 The Protocol’s Cost
sections.text: Across 2430 handoffs in C and D, the protocol took a median of 7.2 ms per handoff (mean 7.5 ms, 95% CI 7.4–7.6 ms; 95th percentile 12.5 ms): 20.5 ms per three-handoff pipeline, or 0.11% of C’s median wall time. A pipeline exchanged 19.5 kB of envelopes on average. Measured end to end, the same quantity is much less precise: the mean per-task difference in wall time between C and B is +0.29 s (95% CI -0.04 to +0.62 s, p = 0.15 p=0.15 ), an interval set by the variance of generation rather than by the protocol. C costs 1.01 × \times as much as B (Table 3 ).

sections.heading: 5.2 Accuracy and Cost
sections.text: Against the uniform pipeline C, the mixed pipeline D changes cost per task by a factor of 0.39 (95% CI 0.38–0.41) and pass@1 by -6.7 percentage points; against the single strong call A, by a factor of 1.27 and -8.1 points. The single cheap call A ′ costs 0.04 × \times as much as A per task, with a pass@1 difference of -24.2 points, and D costs 32.0 × \times as much as A ′ . In the class tier, C’s pass@1 differs from A’s by -2.4 points (95% CI -6.3 to +1.2, p = 0.28 p=0.28 ). In the function tier every condition solves at least 98.7% of runs, so the conditions differ mainly in cost: A ′ solves 98.7% at $0.00019 per solved task, A solves 100.0% at $0.0063, and every pipeline costs more than A for no gain (Fig. 3 ). In the class tier the frontier runs from A ′ through R to A. The cheap model alone solves 52.5% of class-level runs, and no condition solves more than A’s 90.2%. Every pipeline is dominated by A: B and C solve no more at about three times the cost, and D solves fewer at 1.28 × \times A’s cost, its pass@1 differing from C’s by -10.6 points ( p = 0.002 p=0.002 ). Because the reviewer’s output is the graded artefact, the cheap model has the last word in D; the design does not separate how much of that loss comes from the cheap plan and how much from the cheap review.

sections.heading: 5.3 The Model’s Quantities
sections.text: Decomposition at a fixed model inflates output volume by α out = 2.95 \alpha_{\mathrm{out}}=2.95 and input volume by α in = 4.89 \alpha_{\mathrm{in}}=4.89 (function tier 4.18 and 5.56; class tier 2.78 and 4.77), against a feasibility ceiling of 1 / r = 40 1/r=40 . D routes f = 0.74 f=0.74 of its output tokens to the cheap model, against a break-even threshold of f ⋆ = 0.68 f^{\star}=0.68 . Holding token volumes at the uniform pipeline’s values, ( 5 ) forecasts D at 1.02 × \times A (0.81 × \times from the output-only approximation ( 3 )); the observed ratio of mean costs is 1.27 × \times , a forecast error of -19%. Under its own model assignment, D inflates output volume by 4.10 and input volume by 5.13 relative to A. Against C, D’s cost ratio splits into a volume factor of 1.32 and a price factor of 0.30, and the coder, D’s one strong-model stage, accounts for 92.9% of D’s cost.

sections.heading: 5.4 Routing
sections.text: R sent 98.0% of function-level runs and 86.7% of class-level runs to the cheap model, and the routing call itself accounted for 15.1% of R’s cost. Of the runs routed to the cheap model, 28.8% failed, an empirical estimate of the misroute rate q q in ( 7 ); of the runs routed to the strong model, 48.6% concerned tasks the cheap single call solved in every repetition. An oracle that knew, per task, which single call solved it more often would reach a pass@1 of 94.3% at $0.0098 per solved task, against 71.4% at $0.0046 for R.

sections.heading: 5.5 Latency
sections.text: Within each condition, output length and wall time correlate at r r between 0.91 and 0.98; across all runs, at r = 0.87 r=0.87 . In the single-call conditions Opus 5.5 produced about 115 output tokens per second of wall time and Haiku 5.5 about 244. D takes 2.60 × \times as long as A per task and 0.80 × \times as long as C.

sections.heading: 5.6 Failures
sections.text: Almost every unsolved run executed and failed at least one test. Across the six conditions, the number of runs that did not execute – because they raised an error before their tests could run, crashed the grader or exceeded the 30-second limit – was 5, of which 0 were timeouts; the number of runs that hit the 16,000-token output limit in any call was 0; and the number of model calls declined by a safety classifier was 1. sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: The protocol is not where the money goes (H1). At 7.2 ms per handoff, three handoffs add about 20.5 ms to a pipeline whose model calls take tens of seconds, and the envelopes carry no billed tokens. Even a hundred times the measured figure – a generous allowance for transport across hosts or organisations – would add about two seconds to a pipeline that takes about twenty. An overhead this small is invisible end to end: the 95% interval of the C-against-B comparison runs from -0.04 to +0.62 s. Arguments about the cost of interoperability protocols are therefore arguments about decomposition and model choice, not about the protocol. α \alpha belongs to the model assignment, not the task (H2). Re-pricing the uniform pipeline’s token volumes under D’s assignment forecast D at 1.02 × \times A; D cost 1.27 × \times . The error lies entirely in volume. The price factor of 0.30 is close to the ( 1 − f ) + f ​ r ≈ 0.28 (1-f)+fr\approx 0.28 that the routed fraction implies, but the volume factor is 1.32: Haiku 5.5 reasons more than Opus 5.5 in the same roles (reasoning is 37.6% of D’s output tokens against 21.9% of C’s), and D’s output volume relative to A rose from 2.95 to 4.10. Anyone using ( 3 ) to plan a deployment has to measure α \alpha under the assignment being considered: with a cheap model that reasons at length, a decomposition that clears the threshold on paper – here f = 0.74 f=0.74 against f ⋆ = 0.68 f^{\star}=0.68 – can cost more than the single call it was meant to undercut. The saving is in routing tasks, not roles (H3). The single cheap call has the lowest cost per solved task in both tiers, as predicted, but cost per solved task is not the whole frontier: on class-level tasks A ′ solves 52.5% of runs against A’s 90.2%. Per-role assignment works at the wrong granularity for these tasks. D pays strong-model prices for every task’s coding stage and cheap-model quality on every task’s plan and review, whereas the tasks themselves divide into those the cheap model solves alone and those it does not. An oracle choosing per task between the two single calls reaches 94.3% at $0.0098 per solved task, half of A’s $0.0198 at A’s accuracy. Our zero-shot router captured the cost but not the accuracy: it sent 86.7% of class-level runs to the cheap model, and 28.8% of all runs it routed there failed. Routing whole tasks needs no inter-agent protocol at all. Decomposition bought no accuracy (H4). On class-level tasks C’s pass@1 differed from A’s by -2.4 points (95% CI -6.3 to +1.2), at 3.22 × \times the cost and 3.24 × \times the time. For a model as capable as Opus 5.5 on self-contained tasks of this size, a separate planner and reviewer add tokens without adding information the single call lacked. Whether that holds for under-specified or longer-horizon tasks, where a reviewer has real work to do, is the open question. Implications for voice agents. The two parts of the coordination tax weigh differently in a spoken conversation, where a pipeline’s wall time is time the user spends waiting for a reply. The protocol’s share, about 20.5 ms per three-handoff pipeline on one host, is far below what a listener would notice within a turn. Decomposition is not: the uniform pipeline took 3.24 × \times as long as the single call, and moving two roles to the faster cheap model still left the mixed pipeline at 2.60 × \times . For voice agents the latency condition ( 6 ), not the cost condition, is the binding one. A voice agent built on an interoperability protocol can therefore afford the protocol; whether it can afford a deep role decomposition behind every turn is a separate design decision, and the threshold and measurements above let a designer make it before deployment. Whatever the cost results, they speak to only one half of the case for interoperability protocols. The other half rests on capabilities this study does not measure – per-role backends, discovery, fault tolerance, audit trails and composition across organisational boundaries – and those claims deserve measurement rather than assertion (Section 8 ).

sections.heading: 7 Threats to Validity
sections.text: Task sample and contamination. The 135 tasks come from two public benchmarks that the models have likely seen in training. Contamination inflates absolute pass rates for every condition alike; comparisons are paired by task, so it threatens the level of the results more than the differences between conditions. The two tiers support tier-level comparisons, not claims about narrower task types. Some benchmark tests also check behaviour the specification does not state: in ClassEval_0, for example, the docstring promises a boolean while one test expects None , which the reference solution returns only by falling through. We use the benchmarks unchanged; such tests cap pass@1 for every condition alike rather than favouring one. Repetitions are not tasks. Repeated runs of one prompt measure sampling noise. All inference treats the task as the unit; the run count describes the measurement effort, not the sample size. Provider-side variance. Latency for hosted models depends on load conditions outside experimental control. Interleaved randomised execution prevents drift from aliasing onto conditions but does not make absolute latencies reproducible, and the measurements come from one run over two days, with the pauses described in Section 4.5 . Price volatility. The ratio r r is a commercial parameter that changes without notice. The model is stated in terms of r r , so any specific price list is an instantiation of it rather than a finding. Implementation dependence of τ \tau . The measured protocol overhead belongs to one implementation – the OFP Python package behind a Flask server – on one host, not to the specification. It is a lower bound for deployments that cross hosts, networks or organisations. Reasoning defaults. Whether and how much a model reasons when a request does not say is a vendor default that differs between models and model versions. A comparison that leaves it unspecified compares defaults as well as models; we fix effort explicitly and report reasoning tokens per call. The reviewer’s output is graded. In B, C and D the reviewer can repair the coder’s mistakes or introduce new ones. This is a design choice that favours a strong reviewer; in D, the cheap model has the last word on every artefact. The router. R is a zero-shot prompt router. A trained router such as RouteLLM [ 20 ] may route better; the oracle in Section 5.4 bounds what any router could achieve with these two models on these tasks. Provider monoculture and task family. Both models come from one vendor, so protocol effects cannot be separated from vendor-specific serving behaviour, and all tasks are code generation, chosen because correctness is executable and therefore not judged by a model. Where quality must be assessed without execution, LLM-judge protocols carry known biases [ 24 ] .

sections.heading: 8 Future Work
sections.text: The study measures one protocol on one host, and four extensions follow directly. A second protocol : running C and D over A2A as well would turn a single-protocol measurement into a comparative one and guard against attributing an implementation cost to protocol design. Distance : repeating the protocol measurement across hosts and networks would replace the lower bound with deployment figures. Capabilities : fault recovery (terminating an agent mid-task and measuring floor reassignment), fan-out over independent subtasks, the one regime in which a multi-agent architecture can beat a single call on wall time, and discovery (adding a capability through an Assistant Manifest rather than a redeployment) are the claims that motivate interoperability protocols and remain unquantified. Harder tasks : a tier of deliberately under-specified requirements, a second model provider, a trained router, and a length-controlled ablation that re-runs the strong model under the cheap model’s output budget would test whether the volume factor is paid for in quality.

sections.heading: 9 Reproducibility
sections.text: The harness, the task suite together with the builder and pinned dataset hashes that produced it, the raw run log, the two discarded runs, and the analysis script that generates every number, table and figure in Sections 5 and 6 are released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/azettl/coordination-tax-harness . The run log holds one row per run and, for every call within it, the model, input, output and reasoning tokens, cost, model-call time and protocol time, so that any reader can recompute the comparison, including in directions unfavourable to the protocol under test. A dry-run mode exercises the whole harness, including the OFP agent processes and the grader, without calling a model.

sections.heading: 10 Conclusion
sections.text: The question practitioners ask about agent interoperability protocols such as OFP or A2A – are they slower and more expensive than just calling the model? – has no answer as posed, because it holds fixed the one degree of freedom that decomposition buys. Reframed as an economic question, it becomes tractable: decomposition pays when the heterogeneity dividend α ​ f ​ ( 1 − r ) \alpha f(1-r) exceeds the decomposition tax α − 1 \alpha-1 , which yields an explicit threshold on the routable fraction and a hard feasibility ceiling at α = 1 / r \alpha=1/r beyond which no routing policy suffices. The latency version of the condition carries an additive protocol term with no cheap-model analogue, and is therefore strictly harder to satisfy. Because the model is stated in terms of α \alpha , f f and r r rather than of any protocol’s internals, it applies unchanged to A2A or any other inter-agent protocol; only the per-handoff tax τ \tau has to be measured anew. Measured on 135 code-generation tasks with OFP as the protocol under test, the costs separate cleanly. The protocol contributes 7.2 ms per handoff and nothing to the bill. Decomposition contributes most of it – about three times the single call’s cost and time, with no gain in accuracy – and moving roles to a cheap model recovers part of the cost while losing accuracy, because a cheap model that reasons at length raises the very token volume the threshold depends on. The saving that heterogeneous models offer is real, but on these tasks it belongs to choosing a model per task, and a protocol that makes per-role assignment easy, whether OFP, A2A or another, does not by itself capture it.

Comparing such a pipeline with one model call is underspecified, because a pipeline can give each role a different model. We give a closed-form model that sets the coordination tax – decomposition overhead plus per-handoff protocol cost – against the heterogeneity dividend from routing work to a cheaper model, with a break-even threshold and a feasibility bound, α < 1 / r \alpha<1/r , and measure every term, with OFP as the protocol under test, on 135 HumanEval and ClassEval tasks in 2430 runs of six architectures with Claude Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. The protocol adds 7.2 ms per handoff, 0.11% of pipeline wall time. Decomposition does not pay on these tasks: a planner–coder–reviewer pipeline costs 3.22 × \times as much as a single strong call, takes 3.24 × \times as long, and solves no more tasks. Moving planner and reviewer to the cheap model cuts the pipeline’s cost to 0.39 × \times but changes pass@1 by -6.7 points, leaving it dearer, slower and less accurate than the single call, and the break-even forecast misses by -19% because the cheap roles inflate token volume. The saving lies in choosing a model per task instead: an oracle choice between the two single calls solves 94.3% of runs at half the strong call’s cost per solved task. Keywords: Multi-agent LLM systems, Voice agents, Agent interoperability, Open Floor Protocol, LLM routing, Cost-aware evaluation, Benchmarking, Agent Harness 1 Introduction Interoperability protocols for autonomous agents are arriving faster than the evidence for them. The Open Floor Protocol (OFP) [ 22 ] standardises a conversational floor over which heterogeneous agents exchange JSON envelopes; A2A [ 18 ] standardises peer-to-peer agent task delegation; the Model Context Protocol [ 1 ] standardises the agent-to-tool boundary. Each is argued for on the same grounds: agents built on different stacks can discover one another, compose across organisational boundaries, and be replaced independently. Each is deployed on the tacit assumption that the runtime price of that flexibility is small enough not to matter. The assumption is rarely tested. Practitioners ask a blunter question instead – is a multi-agent pipeline simply slower and more expensive than one call to the model? – and the answer usually offered is a benchmark number for one task, one model and one architecture. The question matters most for voice agents. OFP grew out of the effort to let conversational and voice assistants from different vendors work together [ 21 , 7 , 9 ] , and a voice agent is judged turn by turn: whatever time the agents spend coordinating behind the scenes delays the spoken reply the user is waiting for. For such agents latency counts as much as spend, and any overhead that a protocol or a decomposition adds is paid inside the conversational turn. That comparison conflates three mechanisms that move cost in different directions and at different magnitudes. Decomposition splits one generation into several, re-establishing context at every stage and inflating total token volume. The protocol layer adds serialisation, envelope construction, transport and floor management at every handoff. Model heterogeneity allows each role to be served by a different model, so that mechanical roles can be pushed onto cheaper and faster models while only the roles that need frontier capability pay frontier prices. Only the third mechanism can be negative, and it is available exclusively to the decomposed architecture. A benchmark that holds the model fixed across pipeline stages therefore measures the cost of decomposition and the protocol tax while deliberately discarding the only source of saving – and then reports the sum as the cost of the protocol. This paper reframes the question as an economic one. We ask under what conditions the heterogeneity dividend exceeds the coordination tax, derive those conditions in closed form, and measure every parameter in them. The target is a statement of the form: for a decomposition overhead of α \alpha , a cheap/strong price ratio of r r , and a routable work fraction f f , protocol-mediated decomposition is cheaper than a single strong call if and only if f f exceeds an explicit threshold – and is never cheaper, at any f f , once α \alpha exceeds 1 / r 1/r . That statement is protocol-agnostic and survives the next protocol, which a raw benchmark number does not. It is also falsifiable, and we test it. Our contributions are: • a closed-form model of the coordination tax and the heterogeneity dividend, with a cost break-even threshold, a feasibility bound, a latency condition and a misrouting term, and a reporting rule that splits any heterogeneous-versus-uniform cost ratio into a volume factor and a price factor (Section 3 ); • a six-condition design that separates decomposition, protocol and model assignment, and includes the two baselines an economic claim has to beat: one call on the cheap model, and a router (Section 4 ); • a direct measurement of an interoperability protocol’s per-handoff runtime overhead, timed inside the convener rather than inferred from end-to-end differences (Section 5 ); • results on 135 tasks in two difficulty tiers, analysed with the task as the unit and against hypotheses fixed before data collection (Sections 4 – 6 ). Section 2 positions the work, Section 3 develops the model, Section 4 specifies the study, and Sections 5 and 6 report and discuss the results. Sections 7 – 9 cover validity, future work and reproducibility. 2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Agent Interoperability Protocols The Open Floor Protocol, developed within the Open Voice Interoperability Initiative of the Linux Foundation AI & Data Foundation, standardises the Conversation Envelope that every agent sends and receives, Dialog Events representing what was said, Assistant Manifests describing what an agent can do, and a set of floor management events – requestFloor , grantFloor , revokeFloor , yieldFloor – by which agents built by different teams on different stacks take turns in a shared conversation [ 22 , 21 , 2 ] . Its organising metaphor is multi-party conversation: agents gather around a shared floor, and floor management – who holds it, who is invited, who is delegated to – is part of the protocol rather than of the application. This is a deliberate departure from point-to-point delegation models, and it is the feature that makes mid-task reassignment expressible at the protocol level rather than at the orchestrator level; the conception of conversational agency underlying that choice is developed in [ 15 ] . The Assistant Manifest gives discovery a declarative form, so that adding a capability is in principle a manifest change rather than a redeployment. Extensions to the floor model for managing multiparty conversations among heterogeneous assistants are developed in [ 7 , 9 ] , which sets out the delegation and convening semantics the present pipelines rely on, building on the universal open APIs for agentic multimodal communication proposed in [ 10 ] . The intellectual ancestry runs through agent communication languages such as FIPA ACL [ 6 ] , which likewise separated message structure and interaction protocol from agent internals. The modern reprise differs in that the agents are stochastic, the cost of a message is dominated by inference rather than transport, and the price of a message varies by two orders of magnitude depending on which model is behind it. That last property is what makes the economics non-trivial, and it has no analogue in the classical literature. 2.2 Cost-Aware Serving: Cascades and Routers A parallel line of work treats model choice itself as the optimisation variable. FrugalGPT [ 3 ] cascades queries through progressively more expensive models with a learned stopping rule, reporting large cost reductions at matched quality. RouteLLM [ 20 ] trains a router that dispatches each query to a strong or a weak model based on predicted difficulty. Both establish that heterogeneous serving is where the money is; neither involves decomposition, an inter-agent protocol, or more than one model per query. Semantic caching is a third lever on the same cost function, reducing generated volume rather than unit price [ 19 , 14 , 13 ] ; it is orthogonal to the comparison studied here and we hold it out of all conditions, but it shares the property, central to Section 3.7 , that savings in token volume and savings in token price must be accounted separately. This literature supplies the competitor that agent-protocol benchmarks almost always omit. If the object is to save money by using a cheaper model where a cheaper model suffices, a single-call router achieves that with no decomposition overhead and no protocol tax whatsoever. Any claim that multi-agent routing is economically motivated must therefore be made against a router baseline, not against a single strong call. We treat its omission as the central methodological gap in existing comparisons. 2.3 Multi-Agent LLM Frameworks and Their Evaluation Frameworks such as AutoGen [ 23 ] and MetaGPT [ 16 ] popularised role-structured pipelines – planner, implementer, reviewer – and report quality gains on reasoning and code generation. Evaluation in this literature is predominantly quality-first, with cost and latency reported as secondary descriptive statistics when reported at all. Kapoor et al. [ 17 ] document the consequence: agent evaluations that do not control for cost systematically favour architectures that simply spend more inference, and accuracy-only leaderboards reward this. Their prescription – report the accuracy-cost frontier rather than a point – is the one we adopt, extended to latency and to the protocol layer specifically. Work on staged agent pipelines with explicit inter-agent measurement is closer to our setting. An OFP-mediated three-stage pipeline is instrumented in [ 12 ] so that an evaluator observes the full trace without sitting in the decision path, precisely in order to make the protocol boundary measurable rather than implicit; related work on sentinel agents in multi-agent systems [ 11 ] adopts the same separation between the agents doing the work and the agents observing it, and the Agent Status Protocol [ 8 ] proposes a lightweight specification through which agents report their state to such observers. The present study extends that instrumentation from a single pipeline to a controlled comparison of architectures and model assignments. 2.4 The Gap What remains absent from the literature, to our knowledge, is a design that separates decomposition, protocol and model assignment as independent factors; that times the protocol’s per-handoff overhead directly instead of inferring it from noisy end-to-end differences; that includes the cheap single call and the router against which an economic claim must be made; and that evaluates on many tasks with quality off its ceiling, reporting cost per solved task rather than per attempt. That is the gap this study addresses. A comparison across protocols, and the fault-recovery, fan-out and discovery properties that motivate interoperability protocols in the first place, remain future work (Section 8 ). 3 An Analytical Model of the Coordination Tax 3.1 Notation Consider a pipeline of k k stages with H H handoffs, where stage i i runs model m i m_{i} , consumes 𝑖𝑛 i \mathit{in}_{i} input tokens and emits o i o_{i} output tokens, reasoning tokens included: they are billed and generated as output although they never appear in the response. A issues one call to the strong model and A ′ one call to the cheap model. R is a router: the cheap model, at low reasoning effort, reads the task and answers SMALL or LARGE, and the chosen model then gets one call; any answer other than a clear SMALL goes to the strong model. B decomposes the task into three roles – planner, coder, reviewer – chained by direct API calls with no protocol layer. C runs the same three roles over OFP: each specialist is an independent BotAgent in its own process on its own port, exchanging Envelope, GrantFloorEvent, UtteranceEvent and YieldFloorEvent objects from the OFP Python package with a convener over HTTP. D is C with the cheap model as planner and reviewer and the strong model as coder. B, C and D use identical role prompts, and in all three the reviewer’s output is the code that is graded, so in D the final code passes through the cheap model. The design isolates one mechanism per contrast. B against A measures decomposition at a fixed model; C against B measures the protocol at fixed decomposition and model; D against C measures model assignment at a fixed architecture. The function tier draws on HumanEval [ 4 ] : one function per task, specified by its signature and docstring and graded by the task’s own check function. The class tier draws on ClassEval [ 5 ] : one class per task with several methods sharing state, specified by a skeleton with docstrings and graded by the task’s unittest classes. Decomposition has more to do in the class tier, where a plan has to cover several interacting methods. Only ClassEval tasks whose solution and tests need nothing beyond the Python standard library are eligible (88 of 100). Every reference solution was run through the grader before use – twice, or fifty times for tasks that use the random module – and tasks that did not pass every time were dropped: three ClassEval tasks, whose tests depend on the current date, the machine’s hostname and a random draw. The class tier is all 85 remaining tasks, so it involves no sampling choice; the function tier is 50 of HumanEval’s 164 tasks, drawn with a fixed seed. Both downloads are pinned by SHA-256 hash. Each spec wraps the task in one instruction line before and one after, asking for the complete code and nothing else. Generated code is graded in a separate Python process, in a fresh temporary directory, with a 30-second timeout; a run counts as solved only if every test passes. 4.3 Models, Prices and Reasoning The strong model is Claude Opus 5.5, at $4/$20 per million input/output tokens, and the cheap model Claude Haiku 5.5, at $0.10/$0.50, 1 1 1 Standard first-party API prices, https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing , accessed 15 October 2026. Neither model accepts non-default sampling parameters, so repetitions sample each model’s default stochasticity. Output is capped at 16,000 tokens per call, and no prompt caching is used. 4.4 Measuring the Protocol The convener timestamps each handoff from just before it builds the request envelope to just after it has parsed the reply. The receiving agent reports how long its model call took, and the difference is the protocol’s share of that handoff: envelope construction, JSON serialisation, the HTTP round trip, the agent’s event dispatch and floor handling, and the reply envelope. All agents run as separate processes on one host and are started once for the whole run, so process start-up never falls inside a measured handoff. Loopback HTTP without TLS or authentication is the best case for any protocol, so the measurement is a lower bound on what a cross-host or cross-organisation deployment pays. 4.5 Execution and Analysis Each task is run 3 times under each condition, 2430 runs in all. The run proceeds in rounds: each round holds one repetition of every (task, condition) pair in a fresh random order, so that drift in provider-side latency over the hours of the run cannot line up with any condition, and a spending cap fixed in advance can only ever cut the last round short. Runs are written as they complete, and an interrupted run resumes without repeating finished work. The run paused once when the account’s API usage limit was reached and resumed without loss. In two runs a model request hung while the host was asleep and hit the client’s 10-minute timeout before a retry succeeded; their wall time measured the host rather than the model, so both were discarded and re-run, and their $0.07 is not included in the totals. The unit of analysis is the task, not the run: repetitions of one prompt measure sampling noise, not generalisation. Each task’s cost, wall time and solve rate are first averaged over its repetitions. Comparisons between conditions are paired by task. At 7.2 ms per handoff, three handoffs add about 20.5 ms to a pipeline whose model calls take tens of seconds, and the envelopes carry no billed tokens. Even a hundred times the measured figure – a generous allowance for transport across hosts or organisations – would add about two seconds to a pipeline that takes about twenty. An overhead this small is invisible end to end: the 95% interval of the C-against-B comparison runs from -0.04 to +0.62 s. Arguments about the cost of interoperability protocols are therefore arguments about decomposition and model choice, not about the protocol. α \alpha belongs to the model assignment, not the task (H2). Re-pricing the uniform pipeline’s token volumes under D’s assignment forecast D at 1.02 × \times A; D cost 1.27 × \times . The error lies entirely in volume. The price factor of 0.30 is close to the ( 1 − f ) + f ​ r ≈ 0.28 (1-f)+fr\approx 0.28 that the routed fraction implies, but the volume factor is 1.32: Haiku 5.5 reasons more than Opus 5.5 in the same roles (reasoning is 37.6% of D’s output tokens against 21.9% of C’s), and D’s output volume relative to A rose from 2.95 to 4.10. Anyone using ( 3 ) to plan a deployment has to measure α \alpha under the assignment being considered: with a cheap model that reasons at length, a decomposition that clears the threshold on paper – here f = 0.74 f=0.74 against f ⋆ = 0.68 f^{\star}=0.68 – can cost more than the single call it was meant to undercut. The saving is in routing tasks, not roles (H3). The single cheap call has the lowest cost per solved task in both tiers, as predicted, but cost per solved task is not the whole frontier: on class-level tasks A ′ solves 52.5% of runs against A’s 90.2%. Per-role assignment works at the wrong granularity for these tasks. D pays strong-model prices for every task’s coding stage and cheap-model quality on every task’s plan and review, whereas the tasks themselves divide into those the cheap model solves alone and those it does not. An oracle choosing per task between the two single calls reaches 94.3% at $0.0098 per solved task, half of A’s $0.0198 at A’s accuracy. Our zero-shot router captured the cost but not the accuracy: it sent 86.7% of class-level runs to the cheap model, and 28.8% of all runs it routed there failed. Routing whole tasks needs no inter-agent protocol at all. Decomposition bought no accuracy (H4). On class-level tasks C’s pass@1 differed from A’s by -2.4 points (95% CI -6.3 to +1.2), at 3.22 × \times the cost and 3.24 × \times the time. For a model as capable as Opus 5.5 on self-contained tasks of this size, a separate planner and reviewer add tokens without adding information the single call lacked. Whether that holds for under-specified or longer-horizon tasks, where a reviewer has real work to do, is the open question. Implications for voice agents. The two parts of the coordination tax weigh differently in a spoken conversation, where a pipeline’s wall time is time the user spends waiting for a reply. The protocol’s share, about 20.5 ms per three-handoff pipeline on one host, is far below what a listener would notice within a turn. Decomposition is not: the uniform pipeline took 3.24 × \times as long as the single call, and moving two roles to the faster cheap model still left the mixed pipeline at 2.60 × \times . For voice agents the latency condition ( 6 ), not the cost condition, is the binding one. A voice agent built on an interoperability protocol can therefore afford the protocol; whether it can afford a deep role decomposition behind every turn is a separate design decision, and the threshold and measurements above let a designer make it before deployment. Whatever the cost results, they speak to only one half of the case for interoperability protocols. The other half rests on capabilities this study does not measure – per-role backends, discovery, fault tolerance, audit trails and composition across organisational boundaries – and those claims deserve measurement rather than assertion (Section 8 ). 7 Threats to Validity Task sample and contamination. The 135 tasks come from two public benchmarks that the models have likely seen in training. Contamination inflates absolute pass rates for every condition alike; comparisons are paired by task, so it threatens the level of the results more than the differences between conditions. The two tiers support tier-level comparisons, not claims about narrower task types. Some benchmark tests also check behaviour the specification does not state: in ClassEval_0, for example, the docstring promises a boolean while one test expects None , which the reference solution returns only by falling through. We use the benchmarks unchanged; such tests cap pass@1 for every condition alike rather than favouring one. Repetitions are not tasks. Repeated runs of one prompt measure sampling noise. All inference treats the task as the unit; the run count describes the measurement effort, not the sample size. Provider-side variance. Latency for hosted models depends on load conditions outside experimental control. Interleaved randomised execution prevents drift from aliasing onto conditions but does not make absolute latencies reproducible, and the measurements come from one run over two days, with the pauses described in Section 4.5 . Price volatility. The ratio r r is a commercial parameter that changes without notice. The model is stated in terms of r r , so any specific price list is an instantiation of it rather than a finding. Implementation dependence of τ \tau . The measured protocol overhead belongs to one implementation – the OFP Python package behind a Flask server – on one host, not to the specification. It is a lower bound for deployments that cross hosts, networks or organisations. Reasoning defaults. Whether and how much a model reasons when a request does not say is a vendor default that differs between models and model versions. A comparison that leaves it unspecified compares defaults as well as models; we fix effort explicitly and report reasoning tokens per call. The reviewer’s output is graded. In B, C and D the reviewer can repair the coder’s mistakes or introduce new ones. This is a design choice that favours a strong reviewer; in D, the cheap model has the last word on every artefact. The router. R is a zero-shot prompt router. A trained router such as RouteLLM [ 20 ] may route better; the oracle in Section 5.4 bounds what any router could achieve with these two models on these tasks. Provider monoculture and task family. Both models come from one vendor, so protocol effects cannot be separated from vendor-specific serving behaviour, and all tasks are code generation, chosen because correctness is executable and therefore not judged by a model. Where quality must be assessed without execution, LLM-judge protocols carry known biases [ 24 ] . 8 Future Work The study measures one protocol on one host, and four extensions follow directly. A second protocol : running C and D over A2A as well would turn a single-protocol measurement into a comparative one and guard against attributing an implementation cost to protocol design. Distance : repeating the protocol measurement across hosts and networks would replace the lower bound with deployment figures. Capabilities : fault recovery (terminating an agent mid-task and measuring floor reassignment), fan-out over independent subtasks, the one regime in which a multi-agent architecture can beat a single call on wall time, and discovery (adding a capability through an Assistant Manifest rather than a redeployment) are the claims that motivate interoperability protocols and remain unquantified. Harder tasks : a tier of deliberately under-specified requirements, a second model provider, a trained router, and a length-controlled ablation that re-runs the strong model under the cheap model’s output budget would test whether the volume factor is paid for in quality. 9 Reproducibility The harness, the task suite together with the builder and pinned dataset hashes that produced it, the raw run log, the two discarded runs, and the analysis script that generates every number, table and figure in Sections 5 and 6 are released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/azettl/coordination-tax-harness . The run log holds one row per run and, for every call within it, the model, input, output and reasoning tokens, cost, model-call time and protocol time, so that any reader can recompute the comparison, including in directions unfavourable to the protocol under test. A dry-run mode exercises the whole harness, including the OFP agent processes and the grader, without calling a model. 10 Conclusion The question practitioners ask about agent interoperability protocols such as OFP or A2A – are they slower and more expensive than just calling the model? – has no answer as posed, because it holds fixed the one degree of freedom that decomposition buys. Reframed as an economic question, it becomes tractable: decomposition pays when the heterogeneity dividend α ​ f ​ ( 1 − r ) \alpha f(1-r) exceeds the decomposition tax α − 1 \alpha-1 , which yields an explicit threshold on the routable fraction and a hard feasibility ceiling at α = 1 / r \alpha=1/r beyond which no routing policy suffices. The latency version of the condition carries an additive protocol term with no cheap-model analogue, and is therefore strictly harder to satisfy. Because the model is stated in terms of α \alpha , f f and r r rather than of any protocol’s internals, it applies unchanged to A2A or any other inter-agent protocol; only the per-handoff tax τ \tau has to be measured anew. Measured on 135 code-generation tasks with OFP as the protocol under test, the costs separate cleanly. The protocol contributes 7.2 ms per handoff and nothing to the bill. Decomposition contributes most of it – about three times the single call’s cost and time, with no gain in accuracy – and moving roles to a cheap model recovers part of the cost while losing accuracy, because a cheap model that reasons at length raises the very token volume the threshold depends on. The saving that heterogeneous models offer is real, but on these tasks it belongs to choosing a model per task, and a protocol that makes per-role assignment easy, whether OFP, A2A or another, does not by itself capture it.
